reading.text: From next Monday, you can rent a bike at twelve new stations across the city centre. Download the CityBike app, choose a bike and unlock it with your phone. reading.title: Gardens in the sky
reading.text:
In many big cities there is very little space for parks, so some people are looking up instead of out. Rooftop gardens are becoming popular on offices, schools and apartment buildings. Supporters say they have several benefits. Plants on a roof help to keep the building cooler in summer and warmer in winter, which can reduce energy bills. They also absorb rainwater, so less water runs into the streets during storms. Some gardens grow vegetables, which are sold to local restaurants or shared among the people who live in the building.

However, rooftop gardens are not suitable for every building. A garden full of wet soil is very heavy, so engineers must first check that the roof is strong enough. Building one can be expensive, and someone has to look after the plants all year round. Even so, many city councils now offer money to help owners who want to turn an empty roof into a green space.

qs.q: Why are people building gardens on roofs?
o: Cities have little space for parks

qs.q: How can a rooftop garden help during storms?
o: It protects the roof from wind

qs.q: What must happen before a garden is built?
o: Engineers must check the roof is strong enough
Restaurants must agree to buy vegetables

qs.q: What is the writer's overall view?
o: Rooftop gardens are useful but have some practical difficulties
Rooftop gardens are too expensive to be worth it
Every building should have a rooftop garden
Rooftop gardens are mainly for restaurants

reading.title: The four-day week
reading.text:
Over the past few years, a number of companies have experimented with a four-day working week, in which staff work fewer hours for the same pay. The idea is not simply to give people a longer weekend. Its supporters argue that when time is limited, employees concentrate harder, waste less of the day in unnecessary meetings and return to work refreshed. In several trials, managers reported that output stayed the same or even rose slightly, while staff said they felt less stressed and were less likely to look for another job.

Critics, however, point out that the results are not as clear-cut as they first appear. Most trials have involved office-based firms that volunteered to take part, and such companies may already have been well organised and enthusiastic about change. It is far less obvious how a hospital, a school or a factory could cut a day without hiring more people. There is also the question of whether the early gains last: when the novelty wears off, will productivity drift back to where it was? Until longer studies are available, many economists believe the four-day week is a promising idea rather than a proven one.

qs.q: According to supporters, why might a shorter week not reduce output?
o: People focus more and waste less time
Staff work longer hours on each day
Meetings become longer and more useful

qs.q: Why do critics question the trial results?
o: The companies that took part may not be typical
Staff were paid less during the trials
Managers did not report any results

qs.q: What does 'when the novelty wears off' mean here?
o: When the change no longer feels new and exciting

qs.q: Which statement best summarises the economists' view?
o: The idea looks good but needs more evidence
The idea works only in hospitals and schools
The idea should be introduced everywhere now

reading.title: The value of forgetting
reading.text:
We tend to treat forgetting as a failure, a sign that the brain has let us down. Yet a growing body of research suggests that, far from being a design flaw, forgetting may be essential to the way memory works. A brain that recorded every detail of every day would be overwhelmed by trivia; the important patterns would be buried under an avalanche of irrelevant specifics. By allowing unimportant information to fade, the brain makes it easier to generalise from experience and to adapt when circumstances change.

This is not to say that all forgetting is beneficial. Losing a name at a crucial moment is merely embarrassing, but the gradual erosion of memory caused by disease is devastating. The point, rather, is that the healthy brain appears to be actively selective, strengthening some connections while allowing others to weaken. Some researchers have gone so far as to argue that the purpose of memory is not to preserve the past at all, but to help us make better decisions about the future. Seen in this light, the details we lose may matter far less than the lessons we keep.

qs.q: What is the main argument of the text?
o: Forgetting can be a useful part of how memory works
Forgetting is always a sign of illness
People should try to remember every detail
Memory is mainly a record of the past

qs.q: Why would remembering everything be a problem, according to the text?
o: Important patterns would be hidden by trivial details
The brain would become physically larger
People would become embarrassed more often

qs.q: How does the writer treat memory loss caused by disease?
o: As clearly different from healthy forgetting
As another example of useful forgetting
As a myth that research has disproved

qs.q: The phrase 'Seen in this light' introduces…
o: a conclusion based on the view just described

writing.prompt: Write a message to a friend about your last weekend. Say where you went, who you were with and what you did.
